extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students studying metric spaces / introductory topology and analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Expository textbook material giving definitions, propositions, examples, and exercises about metric-space topology: open and closed sets, subspace topology, connectedness, closure/interior/boundary, sequences and convergence, Cauchy/completeness, and compactness (including Lebesgue number lemma and sequential compactness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of open set (metric space)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set V ⊂ X is open (in the metric space (X,d)) if for every x ∈ V there exists δ > 0 such that the open ball B(x,δ) is contained in V.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the basic definition used throughout; open balls themselves provide the local neighborhoods. Many statements (e.g., unions, finite intersections) follow from this definition. See Exercise 7.2.14 (interior is union of open balls).

rubrics_metrics.name: Open set axioms (Proposition 7.2.6, (i))
rubrics_metrics.description: The empty set ∅ and X are open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the base cases for the collection of open sets in any metric space; they are stated explicitly as part of the basic properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite intersection of open sets (Proposition 7.2.6, (ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: If V1, V2, ..., Vk are open subsets of X then ⋂_{j=1}^k V_j is open (finite intersection of open sets is open).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: for x in the intersection, take δ = min(δ1,...,δk) where each δj witnesses x ∈ Vj; then B(x,δ) ⊂ each Vj. Note: this fails for arbitrary (infinite) intersections in general (see Example 7.2.7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitrary union of open sets (Proposition 7.2.6, (iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: If {V_λ}_{λ∈I} is any (possibly infinite) collection of open subsets of X, then ⋃_{λ∈I} V_λ is open (union of open sets is open).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For x in the union, x belongs to some V_λ which is open, hence some ball around x lies in that V_λ and therefore in the union. The index set I may be arbitrarily large.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of closed set (via complements)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subset E ⊂ X is closed if its complement E^c is open (equivalently, closed sets satisfy the dual axioms: ∅ and X closed, arbitrary intersections closed, finite unions closed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 7.2.8 records the closed-set analogues of the open-set axioms. Many proofs proceed by taking complements and applying the open-set results (hint in Exercise 7.2.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed-set axioms (Proposition 7.2.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: (i) ∅ and X are closed; (ii) arbitrary intersection of closed sets is closed; (iii) finite union of closed sets is closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These follow from the respective open-set results by taking complements. Use these when constructing closures or demonstrating closedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open ball is open (Proposition 7.2.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any metric space (X,d), x ∈ X and δ > 0, the open ball B(x,δ) is an open set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the triangle inequality: for y ∈ B(x,δ) take α = δ − d(x,y) > 0 and show B(y,α) ⊂ B(x,δ). Note: the analogous statement that a closed ball is closed is left as an exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subspace topology characterization (Proposition 7.2.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let Y ⊂ X with the subspace metric. A set U ⊂ Y is open in Y (subspace topology) iff there exists an open set V ⊂ X such that U = V ∩ Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to transfer open/closed properties between ambient spaces and subspaces (see Exercise 7.2.12 and Proposition 7.2.12). Examples emphasize that openness/closedness depends on ambient space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open/closed in subspace when ambient open/closed (Proposition 7.2.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: (i) If V ⊂ X is open and U ⊂ V, then U is open in the subspace V iff U is open in X. (ii) If E ⊂ X is closed and F ⊂ E then F is closed in the subspace E iff F is closed in X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplifies checking openness/closedness when the ambient set is itself open/closed. Proofs use Proposition 7.2.11 and basic set operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat: ambient metric space matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a set is open or closed depends on the ambient metric space: a set may be open in a subspace but not open in the larger space (or vice versa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple examples highlight this (e.g., [0,1) with different ambient spaces). Always state the ambient space when declaring open/closed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of connected metric space (Definition 7.2.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: A nonempty metric space X is connected if the only subsets that are both open and closed (clopen) are ∅ and X. A subset A ⊂ X is connected if A (with the subspace topology) is connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently, X is disconnected if it can be written as a union of two nonempty disjoint open sets in X. See the discussion and Figure 7.7 for intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation criterion for disconnectedness (Proposition 7.2.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: A nonempty set S ⊂ X is disconnected iff there exist nonempty open sets U1,U2 in X such that S = (U1 ∩ S) ∪ (U2 ∩ S), (U1 ∩ S) and (U2 ∩ S) are disjoint and nonempty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a practical way to show a set is disconnected by finding a separation by open sets in the ambient space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connected subsets of R (Proposition 7.2.16)
rubrics_metrics.description: A nonempty subset S ⊂ R is connected iff S is an interval or a single point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This characterizes connectedness concretely in the real line; proofs use order properties of R and the infimum construction illustrated in Figure 7.8.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of closure (Definition 7.2.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: The closure of A ⊂ X is Ā := intersection of all closed sets containing A (equivalently the smallest closed set containing A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative characterizations follow (see Proposition 7.2.22 and Proposition 7.3.13). If A is closed then Ā = A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure is closed and contains A (Proposition 7.2.19)
rubrics_metrics.description: For A ⊂ X, the closure Ā is closed and A ⊂ Ā; furthermore, if A is closed then Ā = A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate from the definition as an intersection of closed sets and the existence of X as a closed set containing A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neighborhood characterization of closure (Proposition 7.2.22)
rubrics_metrics.description: x ∈ Ā iff for every δ > 0, B(x,δ) ∩ A ≠ ∅ (i.e., every ball around x meets A). Equivalently, x ∉ Ā iff there exists δ > 0 with B(x,δ) ∩ A = ∅.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the practical test for membership in the closure; used frequently in proofs and exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of interior and boundary (Definition 7.2.23)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interior A° := {x ∈ A : ∃ δ>0, B(x,δ) ⊂ A}. Boundary ∂A := Ā \, A° (points that can be approached both from A and A^c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternate view: interior is union of open sets contained in A (Exercise 7.2.14). Boundary points may or may not belong to A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interior open and boundary closed (Proposition 7.2.26)
rubrics_metrics.description: For A ⊂ X, the interior A° is open and the boundary ∂A is closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: interior is union of balls and therefore open; boundary = Ā \, A° is complement of an open set, hence closed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundary characterization (Proposition 7.2.27)
rubrics_metrics.description: x ∈ ∂A iff for every δ > 0, B(x,δ) contains points of A and points of A^c (i.e., every ball around x meets both the set and its complement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently, ∂A = Ā ∩ (A^c)̄ (Corollary 7.2.28). Figure 7.9 illustrates this idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure via sequences (Proposition 7.3.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: A point p ∈ X lies in Ā iff there exists a sequence (x_n) in A with x_n → p (i.e., closure equals set of sequential limits of points in A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a sequential characterization of closure in metric spaces (see Exercise 7.3.1 for completing the proof).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of sequence and boundedness (Definition 7.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence in X is a function x: N → X written (x_n)_{n=1}^∞. The sequence is bounded if ∃ p ∈ X and B ∈ R with d(p,x_n) ≤ B for all n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the set {x_n : n ∈ N} to check boundedness. Boundedness matters in several propositions (e.g., convergent sequences are bounded).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of convergence (Definition 7.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence (x_n) in X converges to p ∈ X if for every ε>0 ∃ M ∈ N such that for all n ≥ M, d(x_n,p) < ε. If so, write lim_{n→∞} x_n = p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the metric definition of limit; Proposition 7.3.11 relates this to the topology: equivalently, eventually x_n ∈ every neighborhood of p.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of limits (Proposition 7.3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: A convergent sequence in a metric space has a unique limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses triangle inequality and the fact d(x,y)=0 implies x=y. Standard epsilon/2 argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergent sequences are bounded (Proposition 7.3.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (x_n) converges in X then (x_n) is bounded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows because eventually all terms lie in a fixed ball around the limit; combine with finitely many initial terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsequences of convergent sequences (Proposition 7.3.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: (i) If x_n → p then every subsequence x_{n_k} → p. (ii) If the K-tail (starting at K) of a sequence converges to p then the whole sequence converges to p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly to extract convergent subsequences and for tail arguments in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Componentwise convergence in Euclidean space (Proposition 7.3.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence x_m in R^n converges iff each coordinate sequence converges in R; limit is the vector of coordinate-limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Euclidean distance and basic inequalities (√n factor). This reduces many arguments in R^n to the one-dimensional case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence-topology equivalence (Proposition 7.3.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence x_n converges to p iff for every open neighborhood U of p there exists M such that for all n ≥ M, x_n ∈ U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tautologically connects metric epsilon-definition to topological neighborhood language and is used to relate closedness to sequences (Proposition 7.3.12).

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed sets contain limits of sequences (Proposition 7.3.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: If E is closed in X and (x_n) is a sequence in E converging to p, then p ∈ E (closed sets are sequentially closed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by contrapositive using openness of the complement and Proposition 7.3.11.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Cauchy sequence (Definition 7.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence (x_n) in (X,d) is Cauchy if for every ε>0 ∃ M such that for all n,k ≥ M, d(x_n,x_k) < ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This internal criterion measures 'eventually close to each other' without reference to a limit. In complete spaces Cauchy ⇔ convergent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergent implies Cauchy (Proposition 7.4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every convergent sequence in a metric space is Cauchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard consequence of the triangle inequality: if x_n → p then for large n,k both are near p, hence near each other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of completeness (Definition 7.4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: A metric space (X,d) is complete if every Cauchy sequence in X converges to a point of X (i.e., every Cauchy has a limit in X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Completeness is a global property of the space (not every subset of a complete space is complete); closed subspaces of complete spaces are complete (Proposition 7.4.6).

rubrics_metrics.name: R^n is complete (Proposition 7.4.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Euclidean space R^n with the standard metric is a complete metric space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces to the one-dimensional completeness of R applied to coordinate sequences; used as a model of complete finite-dimensional spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed subsets of complete spaces are complete (Proposition 7.4.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is complete and E ⊂ X is closed (with the subspace metric) then E is complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intuition: closed sets contain their limit points, so any Cauchy sequence in E that converges in X must have its limit in E.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of compactness (open-cover) (Definition 7.4.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: K ⊂ X is compact if for every open cover {U_λ}_{λ∈I} of K there exists a finite subcollection U_{λ1},...,U_{λm} whose union still covers K (i.e., every open cover has a finite subcover).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard topological definition of compactness. Examples and non-examples are given (R noncompact, closed bounded intervals are compact in R).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact implies closed and bounded (Proposition 7.4.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If K ⊂ X is compact then K is bounded and K is closed (in X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boundedness shown by covering K with balls centered at a point with radii n; closedness shown by taking x in closure but not in K and constructing an open cover of K with no finite subcover. Note: closed+bounded is not sufficient for compactness in general metric spaces (counterexamples in infinite-dimensional or incomplete spaces).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lebesgue covering lemma for sequentially compact sets (Lemma 7.4.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If K is sequentially compact and {U_λ}_{λ∈I} is an open cover of K then there exists δ>0 such that for every x ∈ K there is λ ∈ I with B(x,δ) ⊂ U_λ (i.e., a uniform radius δ works for the cover).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lemma provides a single Lebesgue number δ for the cover; proof by contradiction constructs a sequence that cannot have a convergent subsequence, contradicting sequential compactness. The δ depends on the cover but not on x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequential compactness equivalent to compactness in metric spaces (Theorem 7.4.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: In metric spaces, K is compact iff every sequence in K has a convergent subsequence with limit in K (compact ⇔ sequentially compact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This equivalence is specific to metric spaces (not general topological spaces); the Lebesgue number lemma is a key tool in the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning: closed and bounded need not imply compact in general
rubrics_metrics.description: In general metric spaces (especially infinite-dimensional ones) a set being closed and bounded does not guarantee compactness (e.g., closed unit ball in certain function spaces is not compact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text gives examples and exercises illustrating where closed+bounded fails to imply compact. In finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces closed+bounded ⇔ compact (Heine–Borel), but not in arbitrary metric spaces.
